description: Passages of Vattel's Droit des gens reused in American documents of 1762–1776, found by a search of the corpus below against the English translation (London, 1797) and read twice by language models; each with the French words it renders and the edition's sources for them. Built by tools/american/.

reuses.author: James Otis

reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
W hen a nation takes po/Teffion of a diilant country, and settles a colony there, that country though separated from the 
principal eRablifhment, or mother country, naturally becomes 
a part of the ilate, equally with its antient pofTeffions. W henever the political laws, or treaties, make no dihindion between them, every thing said of the territory of a nation,

reuses.vattel_1797: When a nation takes possession of a distant country, and settles a colony there, that country, though separated from the principal establishment, or mother-country, naturally becomes a part of the state, equally with its ancient possessions. Whenever therefore the political laws, or treaties, make no distinction between them, every thing said of the territory of a nation, must also extend to its colonies.
reuses.french: Lorsqu'une nation s'empare d'un pays éloigné , & y établit une colonie , ce pays , quoique séparé de l'établissement principal , fait naturellement partie de l'état ; tout comme ses anciennes possessions. Toutes les fois donc que les loix politiques ou les traités n'y apportent point de différence , tout ce qui se dit du territoire d'une nation doit s'entendre aussi de ses colonies.
reuses.edition: Otis, Rights (Boston, 1764)
reuses.note: The note, which opens on p. 109 with I.34 (V19), runs on into the whole of I.210 ('antient', 'ought also to extend') and signs it 'D' Vattel', backing the memorial's claim that the colonies are part of the state and that acts against the fundamental principles of the constitution are void. The first judge's reading is right.

reuses.author: Oxenbridge Thacher
reuses.document: The Sentiments of a British American (Boston, 1764)
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.vattel_1797: it has cost rivers of blood; but they have not purchased it too dear
reuses.french: Heureuse constitution ! à laquelle on n'a pu parvenir tout d'un coup , qui a coûté , il est vrai , des ruisseaux de sang , mais que l'on n'a point achetée trop cher.
reuses.edition: Thacher, Sentiments (Boston, 1764)
reuses.note: Thacher cites Vattel's praise of the English constitution to show the British are jealous of their liberties, and argues that the colonists share those rights, which the Sugar Act wounds; he swells Vattel's "rivers" (French "ruisseaux") into "seas" of blood. The judge named the wrong author: the pamphlet is by Oxenbridge Thacher, not James Thacher.

reuses.vattel_1797: It essentially belongs to the society to make laws both in relation to the manner in which it desires to be governed, and to the conduct of the citizens:—this is called the legislative power. The nation may intrust the exercise of it to the prince, or to an assembly; or to that assembly and the prince jointly; who have then a right to make new laws and to repeal old ones. It is asked whether their power extends to the fundamental laws,—whether they may change the constitution of the state? The principles we have laid down lead us to decide with certainty, that the authority of these legislators does not extend so far, and that they ought to consider the fundamental laws as sacred, if the nation has not, in very express terms, given them power to change them. For the constitution of the state ought to possess stability: and since that was first established by the nation, which afterwards intrusted certain persons with the legislative power, the fundamental laws are excepted from their commission. It is visible that the society only intended to make provision for having the state constantly furnished with laws suited to particular conjunctures, and, for that purpose, gave the legislature the power of abrogating the ancient civil and political laws that were not fundamental, and of making new ones: but nothing leads us to think that
reuses.french: Il se présente encore ici une question très - importante. Il appartient essentiellement à la société de faire des loix sur la maniere dont elle prétend être gouvernée , & sur la conduite des citoyens : ce pouvoir s'appelle puissance législative. La nation peut en confier l'exercice au prince , ou à une assemblée , ou à cette assemblée & au prince conjointement ; lesquels sont dès lors en droit de faire des loix nouvelles & d'abroger les anciennes. On demande si leur pouvoir s'étend jusques sur les loix fondamentales , s'ils peuvent changer la constitution de l'état. Les principes que nous avons posés nous conduisent certainement à décider que l'autorité de ces législateurs ne va pas si loin , & que les loix fondamentales doivent être sacrées pour eux , si la nation ne leur a pas donné très - expressément le pouvoir de les changer. Car la constitution de l'état doit être stable : & puisque la nation l'a premiérement établie , & qu'elle a ensuite confié la puissance législative à certaines personnes , les loix fondamentales sont exceptées de leur commission. On voit que la société a seulement voulu pourvoir à ce que l'état fut toujours muni de loix convenables aux conjonctures , & donner pour cet effet aux législateurs le pouvoir d'abroger les anciennes loix civiles & les loix politiques non fondamentales , & d'en faire de nouvelles ; mais rien ne conduit à penser qu'elle ait voulu soumettre sa constitution même à leur volonté.
reuses.edition: Otis, Rights (Boston, 1764)
reuses.note: The note, apparently keyed to 'acts against the fundamental principles of the British constitution are void', reproduces I.34 from 'A very important question here presents itself' to 'submit the constitution itself to their pleasure', so that Parliament cannot change the constitution under which the colonists hold their rights. The judge called it unnamed, but the same note runs straight on into I.210 and is signed 'D' Vattel', so quotation fits better than verbatim.

reuses.edition: Otis, Rights (Boston, 1764)
reuses.note: Otis quotes III.201 at length in the 1760 London translation, from "But if the whole state be conquered" through "the state of war subsists" plus the sentence on a sovereign who would enslave a conquered people, to deny that Parliament could vote the King absolute; the judge's match is only the middle of a longer quotation that runs from p. 111 to p. 112. The French covers the sentence where Vattel calls the conqueror's absolute mastery a monstrous principle, against Wolff, JG §§ 870-871 (and Grotius III.8.1).

reuses.author: John Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
Every 
interpretation that leads to an absurdity, ought to be rejected." 
Page 222, book 2, ch. 17, s. 282. Every impossibility, physical 
and moral, is an absurdity
reuses.vattel_1797: Every interpretation that leads to an absurdity, ought to be rejected; or, in other words, we should not give to any piece a meaning from which any absurd consequences would follow, but must interpret it in such a manner as to avoid absurdity. As it is not to be presumed that any one means what is absurd, it cannot be supposed that the person speaking intended that his words should be understood in a manner from which an absurdity would follow. Neither is it allowable to presume that he meant to indulge a sportive levity in a serious deed: for what is shameful and unlawful is not to be presumed. We call absurd not only what is physically impossible, but what is morally so
reuses.french: Toute interprétation qui mene à l'absurde doit être rejettée
reuses.edition: Works of John Adams, ed. C. F. Adams, II (1850)
reuses.note: Adams quotes II.282's rule against absurd interpretation and adds, outside the marks, his own condensation of Vattel's next sentence ('On appelle absurde, non seulement ce qui est impossible physiquement, mais encore ce qui l'est moralement'), presumably aimed at the impossibility of obtaining stamps. The first judge's reading is right.

reuses.author: John Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
If a case be presented in which one cannot 
absolutely apply the well known reason of a law or a promise, 
this case ought to be excepted
reuses.vattel_1797: if a case occurs, to which the well-known reason of a law or promise is utterly inapplicable, that case ought to be excepted
reuses.french: s'il se présente un cas auquel on ne puisse absolument point appliquer la raison bien connue d'une loi, ou d'une promesse, ce cas doit être excepté
reuses.edition: Works of John Adams, ed. C. F. Adams, II (1850)
reuses.note: Adams copies three of Vattel's rules of interpretation (II.297, II.292, II.282) in the 1760 translation, whose 'If a case be presented in which one cannot absolutely apply' follows the French more closely than the 1797 text, as ammunition for having the courts proceed without stamps by following the lawgiver's reason over the letter. The first judge's reading is right.

reuses.author: John Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
In unforeseen cases, that is, when the state of 
things is found such as the author of the disposition has not 
foreseen, and could not have thought of, we should rather follow 
his intention than his words, and interpret the act as he himself 
would have interpreted it, had he been present, or conformably 
to what he would have done if he had foreseen the things that 
happened. This rule is of great use to Judges
reuses.vattel_1797: In unforeseen cases, that is to say, when the state of things happens to be such as the author of a deed has not foreseen, and could not have thought of, we should rather be guided by his intention than by his words, and interpret the instrument as he himself would interpret it if he were on the spot, or conformably to what he would have done if he had foreseen the circumstances which are at present known. This rule is of great use to judges
reuses.french: Dans les cas imprévus , c'est - à - dire , lorsque l'état des choses se trouve tel , que l'auteur d'une disposition ne l'a point prévu , & n'a pu y penser , il faut suivre plutôt son intention que ses paroles , & interpréter l'acte comme il l'interpréteroit lui - même s'il étoit présent , ou conformément à ce qu'il eut fait , s'il eut prévû les choses que l'on connoît présentement. Cette regle est d'un grand usage pour les juger
reuses.edition: Works of John Adams, ed. C. F. Adams, II (1850)
reuses.note: During the Stamp Act closure of the courts, Adams copies three interpretation rules (II.297, II.292, II.282) with page references to the English translation, to argue that the courts may proceed without stamps. His wording ("author of the disposition", "the act", "had he been present") is the earlier translation's and stays closer to the French than the 1797 text. The judge's reading is right.

reuses.author: Richard Bland
reuses.document: An Inquiry into the Rights of the British Colonies (Williamsburg, 1766)
reuses.label: close paraphrase
reuses.american:
it is evident, by the very Act of 
Association, that each Member subjects himself to the 
Authority of that Body
reuses.vattel_1797: by the very act of the civil or political association, each citizen subjects himself to the authority of the entire body
reuses.french: On conçoit que par l'acte d'association civile ou politique , chaque citoyen se soumet à l'autorité du corps entier
reuses.edition: Bland, Inquiry (Williamsburg, 1766; repr. 1922)
reuses.note: Bland restates Vattel I.2 ("Member" for "citizen", "that Body" for "the entire body") in a social-contract argument: those excluded from the franchise remain bound by implicit consent but keep a natural right to emigrate. The first judge's reading is right.

reuses.author: Richard Bland
reuses.document: An Inquiry into the Rights of the British Colonies (Williamsburg, 1766)
reuses.label: close paraphrase
reuses.american:
lay their Complaints at the Foot of the Throne, and 
to suffer patiently rather than disturb the publick Peace, 
which nothing but a Denial of Justice can excuse them 
in breaking.
reuses.vattel_1797: lay their complaints at the foot of the throne. Every citizen should even patiently endure evils which are not insupportable, rather than disturb the public peace
reuses.french: ils peuvent porter leurs plaintes au pied du trône. Tout citoyen doit même souffrir patiemment des maux supportables, plutôt que de troubler la paix publique. Il n'y a qu'un déni de justice de la part du souverain , ou des délais affectés , qui puissent excuser l'emportement d'un peuple poussé à bout, le justifier même , si les maux sont intolérables , l'oppression grande & manifeste.
reuses.edition: Bland, Inquiry (Williamsburg, 1766; repr. 1922)
reuses.note: Bland follows III.290 through a whole sentence ("great and manifest Oppressions", complaints at the foot of the throne, patient suffering rather than disturbing the peace, excused only by a denial of justice) to set the colonists' remedy for loss of civil rights; the denial-of-justice exception is Vattel's, since the Wolff rows allow petition only. The judge's confidence was too low.

reuses.author: Massachusetts House of Representatives (Samuel Adams)
reuses.document: Letter to the Earl of Shelburne, 15 January 1768
reuses.label: verbatim
reuses.american:
if the Parliament 
should make any considerable change in the constitution, and the 
nation should be voluntarily silent upon it, this would be considered as an approbation of the act
reuses.vattel_1797: if the parliament entered into a debate on making so considerable a change, and the whole nation was voluntarily silent upon it, this would be considered as an approbation of the act
reuses.french: Mais si le parlement délibéroit de faire un changement si considérable , & que la nation entiere gardât volontairement le silence , elle seroit censée approuver le fait de ses réprésentans.
reuses.edition: Bradford, Speeches of the Governors (1818)
reuses.note: The House uses Vattel's point that a nation's silence while Parliament changes the constitution counts as approval to justify its protest against the Townshend duties. The judge left the letter as "a British peer" (it is Shelburne) and missed that p. 138 of the same letter ("In all free states, the constitution is fixed ... it cannot change the constitution without destroying its own foundation") also paraphrases I.34.

reuses.author: Massachusetts House of Representatives (Samuel Adams)
reuses.label: close paraphrase
reuses.american: without the most pressing reason, or an absolute necessity
reuses.vattel_1797: without the most pressing reasons, or an absolute necessity
reuses.french: les grands changemens dans l'état étant des opérations délicates , pleines de dangers , & la fréquence des changemens nuisible en elle - même , un peuple doit être trèscirconspect sur cette matiere , & ne se porter jamais aux nouveautés , sans les raisons les plus pressantes , ou sans nécessité
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, I (1904)
reuses.note: The House calls the Mutiny Act's requisition on the colonies 'a great change; and in its nature delicate', not to be made 'without the most pressing reason, or an absolute necessity', applying Vattel's caution on constitutional change to Parliament. Only a phrase is verbatim, so close paraphrase fits better than verbatim; the letter is the Camden letter, which reuses I.36 a page later.

reuses.author: Massachusetts House of Representatives (Samuel Adams)
reuses.label: close paraphrase
reuses.american:
the nation will judge and determine in conformity to 
its political constitution
reuses.vattel_1797: it belongs to the nation alone to judge and determine them conformably to its political constitution
reuses.french: s'il s'éleve dans l'état des contestations sur les loix fondamentales , sur l'administration publique , sur les droits des différentes puissances qui y ont part , il appartient uniquement à la nation d'en juger & de les terminer conformément à sa constitution politique
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, I (1904)
reuses.note: The House drops Vattel's 'alone' and restates his rule that disputes on the public administration are for the nation to judge by its constitution, then says the end of the British constitution is liberty and appeals to Camden. The judge was right on the substance; the addressee is Lord Camden.

reuses.author: Samuel Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
It is an admirable institution, by which every 
citizen may be plac'd in a situation, that enables him 
to contribute to the great end of society, the dis 
tributing justice ; and it every where diffuses a spirit 
of true patriotism, which is zealously employed for 
the publick welfare.
reuses.vattel_1797: An admirable constitution there places every citizen in a situation that enables him to contribute to this great end, and every-where diffuses that spirit of genuine patriotism which zealously exerts itself for the public welfare
reuses.french: Une constitution admirable y met tout citoyen en état de concourir à cette grande fin , & répand par-tout cet esprit de vrai patriotisme , qui s'occupe avec zele du bien public.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Adams moves Vattel's praise of the English constitution to jury trial: 'constitution' becomes 'institution' and 'this great end' becomes 'the great end of society, the distributing justice', while 'a spirit of true patriotism, which is zealously employed for the publick welfare' keeps the older translation's wording. The marks show a quotation, but the 'great writer' named just before speaks to a different point, so Vattel is not named.

reuses.author: Samuel Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
The constitution and its 
laws are the basis of the public tranquility — the firm 
est support of the public authority, and the pledge of 
the liberty of the citizens : But the constitution is a 
vain Phantom, and the best laws are useless, if they 
are not religiously observed. The nation ought then 
to watch, and the true patriot will watch very atten 
tively, in order to render them equally respected, by 
those who govern, and the people destin'd to obey " — 
To violate the laws of the state is a capital crime ; 
and if those guilty of it, are invested with authority, 
they add to this crime, a perfidious abuse of the 
power with which they are entrusted : " The nation 
therefore, the people, ought to suppress those abuses 
with their utmost care & vigilance
reuses.vattel_1797: The constitution and laws of a state are the basis of the public tranquillity, the firmest support of political authority, and a security for the liberty of the citizens. But this constitution is a vain <10> phantom, and the best laws are useless, if they be not religiously observed: the nation ought then to watch very attentively, in order to render them equally respected by those who govern, and by the people destined to obey. To attack the constitution of the state, and to violate its laws, is a capital crime against society; and if those guilty of it are invested with authority, they add to this crime a perfidious abuse of the power with which they are intrusted. The nation ought constantly to repress them with its utmost vigour and vigilance
reuses.french: La constitution de l'état & ses loix sont la base de la tranquillité publique , le plus ferme appui de l'autorité politique & le gage de la liberté des citoyens. Mais cette constitution est un vain fantôme , & les meilleures loix sont inutiles , si on ne les observe pas religieusement. La nation doit donc veiller sans relâche à les faire également respecter & de ceux qui gouvernent , & du peuple destiné à obéir. Attaquer la constitution de l'état , violer ses loix , c'est un crime capital contre la société ; & si ceux qui s'en rendent coupables sont des personnes revêtues d'autorité , ils ajoutent au crime en lui - même , un perfide abus du pouvoir qui leur est confié. La nation doit constamment les réprimer avec toute la vigueur & la vigilance que demande l'importance du sujet.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Adams quotes I.30 against Philanthrop's call for subordination. He inserts 'and the true patriot will watch' and 'the people' to make the body of the people the guardian of the constitution, and he leaves the middle sentence on violating the laws as a capital crime outside the marks.

reuses.author: Massachusetts House of Representatives (Samuel Adams)
reuses.label: close paraphrase
reuses.american: If ever the provincial assemblies should be voluntarily silent, on the Parliament's taking upon themselves a power thus to violate our constitutional and Charter Rights, it might be considered as an approbation of it, or at least a tacit consent
reuses.vattel_1797: if the parliament entered into a deliberation to make so important a change, and the whole nation was voluntarily silent upon it, this would be considered as an approbation of the act of its representatives
reuses.french: Mais si le parlement délibéroit de faire un changement si considérable , & que la nation entiere gardât volontairement le silence , elle seroit censée approuver le fait de ses réprésentans.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: The House applies the silence clause to the provincial assemblies and concludes: 'It is therefore our duty to declare our Rights'.

reuses.author: Samuel Adams
reuses.label: close paraphrase
reuses.american: If therefore we are voluntarily silent while the single duty on tea is continued, or do any act, however innocent, simply considered, which may be construed by the tools of administration ... as an acquiescence in the measure, we are in extreme hazard
reuses.vattel_1797: if the parliament entered into a deliberation to make so important a change, and the whole nation was voluntarily silent upon it, this would be considered as an approbation of the act of its representatives
reuses.french: Mais si le parlement délibéroit de faire un changement si considérable , & que la nation entiere gardât volontairement le silence , elle seroit censée approuver le fait de ses réprésentans.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Adams applies the silence clause to the remaining tea duty: silence would be construed as acquiescence.

reuses.author: Samuel Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
" By the 
fundamental laws of England, the two houses of par 
liament in concert with the King, exercise the legisla 
tive power : But if the two houses should be so 
infatuated, as to resolve to suppress their powers, and 


i77i] SAMUEL ADAMS. 255 

invest the King with the full and absolute government, 
certainly the nation would not suffer it."
reuses.vattel_1797: By the fundamental laws of England, the two houses of parliament, in concert with the king, exercise the legislative power: but if the two houses should resolve to suppress themselves, and to invest the king with full and absolute authority, certainly the nation would
reuses.french: Par les loix fondamentales de l'Angleterre , les deux chambres du parlement , de concert avec le roi , exercent la puissance législative. S'il prenoit envie aux deux chambres de se supprimer ellesmêmes , & de revêtir le roi de l'empire plein & absolu , certainement la nation ne le souffriroit pas.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Just before the quotation Adams paraphrases the end of I.34 ('if we are voluntarily silent... it will be consider'd as an approbation of the change'). He then quotes Vattel on the two houses, adding 'be so infatuated', and goes from there to the people's right to resist a minister who sets up his instructions to Hutchinson as laws. The judge's 'attrib.' and undated essay is the Candidus article of October 14, 1771.

reuses.author: Samuel Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
Every man being born free, says another distin 
guished writer, the son of a citizen, arrived at the 
years of discretion, may examine whether it be con 
venient for him to join in the society for which he was 
destined by birth*. If he finds that it will be no ad 
vantage for him to remain in it, he is at liberty to 
leave it, preserving as much as his new engagements 
will allow him, the love and gratitude he owes it.
reuses.vattel_1797: But every man is born free; and the son of a citizen, when come to the years of discretion, may examine whether it be convenient for him to join the society for which he was destined by his birth. If he does not find it advantageous to remain in it, he is at liberty to quit it on making it a compensation for what it has done in his favour,* and preserving, as far as his new engagements will allow him, the sentiments of love and gratitude he owes it.
reuses.french: Mais tout homme naît libre ; le fils d'un citoyen, parvenu à l'âge de raison, peut examiner s'il lui convient de se joindre à la société que sa naissance lui destine. S'il ne trouve point qu'il lui soit avantageux d'y rester, il est le maître de la quitter, en la dédommageant de ce qu'elle pourroit avoir fait en sa faveur ( * ), & en conservant pour elle, autant que ses nouveaux engagemens le lui permettront, les sentimens d'amour & de reconnoissance qu'il lui doit.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Adams sets Vattel beside Locke against Hutchinson's claim that allegiance is perpetual and unalienable, and he silently drops the condition that the emigrant compensate the society ('en la dédommageant...'). The words are covered only by Burlamaqui and Pufendorf-Barbeyrac rows. The free right to leave that they state is the point on which Vattel departs from Wolff, Inst. § 1019, which requires the superior's consent.

reuses.author: Samuel Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
There are cases in which a citizen 
has an absolute right to renounce his country, and 
abandon it for ever
reuses.vattel_1797: There are cases in which a citizen has an absolute right to renounce his country, and abandon it entirely
reuses.french: Il est des cas dans lesquels un citoyen est absolument en droit, par des raisons prises du pacte même de la société politique, de renoncer à sa patrie & de l'abandonner.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Adams uses the absolute right to renounce one's country against Hutchinson's perpetual allegiance. He then paraphrases Vattel's third case, the sovereign or majority allowing only one religion, to say the Puritans left England lawfully (covered by Wolff JG § 153, shared argument, and a § 153 divergence). The quoted sentence itself has only a Pufendorf-Barbeyrac note row and is the point Vattel holds against Wolff, JG § 154.

reuses.author: Samuel Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
The 
fundamental laws," says Vatel, " are excepted from 
their (legislators) commission," " nothing leads us to 
think that the nation was willing to submit the cons ft326 THE WRITINGS OF [1772 

tution itself to their pleasure." " They derive their 
authority from the constitution, how then can they 
change it without destroying the foundation of their 
own authority ? "
reuses.vattel_1797: the fundamental laws are excepted from their commission. It is visible that the society only intended to make provision for having the state constantly furnished with laws suited to particular conjunctures, and, for that purpose, gave the legislature the power of abrogating the ancient civil and political laws that were not fundamental, and of making new ones: but nothing leads us to think that it meant to submit the constitution itself to their will. In short, it is from the constitution that those legislators derive their power: how then can they change it, without destroying the foundation of their own authority?
reuses.french: les loix fondamentales sont exceptées de leur commission. On voit que la société a seulement voulu pourvoir à ce que l'état fut toujours muni de loix convenables aux conjonctures , & donner pour cet effet aux législateurs le pouvoir d'abroger les anciennes loix civiles & les loix politiques non fondamentales , & d'en faire de nouvelles ; mais rien ne conduit à penser qu'elle ait voulu soumettre sa constitution même à leur volonté. Enfin , c'est de la constitution que ces législateurs tiennent leur pouvoir ; comment pourroient - ils la changer , sans détruire le fondement de leur autorité ?
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Adams strings together three sentences of I.34 in marks to argue that, as Magna Charta declares the fundamental laws, Parliament cannot alter it and an act against it is void. The same article quotes the earlier part of I.34 (legislators' authority "does not extend so far", fundamental laws "sacred", constitution "fixed") just before and its England example just after, so the whole run on pp. 325-326 quotes nearly all of the section; the wording ("to their pleasure") is the earlier English translation.

reuses.author: Samuel Adams
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
Tyrants alone, 
says the great Vatei, will treat as seditious, those 
brave and resolute citizens, who exhort the people to 
preserve themselves from oppression, in vindication 
of their rights and privileges : A good prince, says 

he, will commend such virtuoiis patriots " and 

will " mistrust the selfish suggestions of a minister, 
who represents to him as rebels, all those citizens who 
do not hold out their hands to chains, who refuse 
tamely to suffer the strokes of arbitrary power."
reuses.vattel_1797: tyrants alone will treat, as seditious, those brave and resolute citizens who exhort the people to preserve themselves from oppression, and to vindicate their rights and privileges: a good prince will commend such virtuous patriots, provided their zeal be tempered with moderation and prudence. If he has justice and his duty at heart,—if he aspires to that immortal and unsullied glory of being the father of his people, let him mistrust the selfish suggestions of that minister who represents to him as rebels all those citizens who do not stretch out their necks to the yoke of slavery,—who refuse tamely to crouch under the rod of arbitrary power.
reuses.french: les tyrans seuls traiteront de séditieux ces citoyens courageux & fermes , qui exhortent le peuple à se garantir de l'oppression, à maintenir ses droits & ses privileges: un bon prince louera ces vertueux patriotes, pourvu que leur zele soit tempéré par la modération & la prudence. S'il aime la justice & son devoir, s'il aspire à la gloire immortelle & si pure d'être le pere de son peuple , qu'il se défie des suggestions intéressées d'un ministre qui lui peint comme des rebelles tous les citoyens qui ne ten-dent pas les mains à l'esclavage, qui refusent de plier sans murmure , sous les coups d'un pouvoir arbitraire.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Adams quotes Vattel to defend jealousy as a political virtue and the "patriots" Chronus derides, silently dropping Vattel's proviso that their zeal be tempered with moderation and prudence. His wording ("in vindication of their rights", "hold out their hands to chains", "suffer the strokes of arbitrary power") follows an earlier English translation closer to the French (tendent les mains à l'esclavage, sous les coups) than the 1797 text; the quotation sits on p. 323 only, not 322-323.

reuses.author: Boston town meeting (Samuel Adams)
reuses.document: The State of the Rights of the Colonists, 20 November 1772
reuses.label: close paraphrase
reuses.american:
A Common Wealth or state is a body politick or 
civil society of men, united together to promote their 
mutual safety and prosperity, by means of their 
union.*
reuses.vattel_1797: a body politic, or a society of men united together for the purpose of promoting their mutual safety and advantage by their combined strength
reuses.french: un corps politique, ou une société d'hommes unis ensemble pour procurer leur avantage & leur sûreté , à forces réunies.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: Adams opens the colonists' rights as subjects with Vattel's definition of the state, grafting Locke's "Common Wealth" and "civil society" onto it (hence the note "See Lock and Vatel") and rendering "à forces réunies" as "by means of their union", apparently the earlier English translation. The I.1 form fits better than Prelim.1 (V32), which it restates; behind both lies Wolff's definition of civitas (Jus gentium § 9).

reuses.author: Thomas Hutchinson
reuses.document: Speech to the two Houses, 6 January 1773
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
when a nation takes possession of a distant 
country, and settles there, that country, though separated from the

reuses.vattel_1797: When a nation takes possession of a distant country, and settles a colony there, that country, though separated from the principal establishment, or mother-country, naturally becomes a part of the state, equally with its ancient possessions.
reuses.french: Lorsqu'une nation s'empare d'un pays éloigné , & y établit une colonie , ce pays , quoique séparé de l'établissement principal , fait naturellement partie de l'état ; tout comme ses anciennes possessions.
reuses.edition: Bradford, Speeches of the Governors (1818)
reuses.note: Hutchinson quotes I.210 to argue that the colony, as a settlement of the nation, has always been subject to Parliament's supreme authority. He drops "a colony" after "settles"; his "or mother country" is in the English translation only (the French has just "l'établissement principal"), so he used the English Vattel.

as the fundamentals of the constitution. They ought

reuses.vattel_1797: does not extend so far, and that they ought to consider the fundamental laws as sacred, if the nation has not, in very express terms, given them power to change them. For the constitution of the state ought to possess stability: and since that was first established by the nation, which afterwards intrusted certain persons with the legislative power, the fundamental laws are excepted from their commission
reuses.french: l'autorité de ces législateurs ne va pas si loin , & que les loix fondamentales doivent être sacrées pour eux , si la nation ne leur a pas donné très - expressément le pouvoir de les changer. Car la constitution de l'état doit être stable : & puisque la nation l'a premiérement établie , & qu'elle a ensuite confié la puissance législative à certaines personnes , les loix fondamentales sont exceptées de leur commission.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: The House quotes I.34 to argue that the fundamentals of the province's constitution are fixed in the charter, so no provincial acts referring to acts of Parliament can be taken as conceding Parliament's supreme authority. The date is 26 January 1773; the wording ("fixed", "trusted") is the earlier English translation.

reuses.author: Massachusetts House of Representatives
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american: The celebrated author, whom your Excellency has quoted, tells us, that, " neither the one or the other of the interested, or contracting powers, hath a right to interpret at pleasure."
reuses.vattel_1797: Neither the one nor the other of the parties interested in the contract has a right to interpret the deed or treaty according to his own fancy.
reuses.french: ni l'un ni l'autre des intéressés, ou des contractans n'est en droit d'interpréter à son gré l'acte, ou le traité.
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: The House turns the Governor's author against him: Parliament, even as a party to the charter, could not interpret it at pleasure. The wording is not the 1797 translation's.

reuses.author: Massachusetts House of Representatives
reuses.label: quotation
reuses.american:
An agreement ought to be in 
terpreted " in such a manner as that it may have its 
effect."
reuses.vattel_1797: in such a manner, as that it may have its effect
reuses.french: Il faut l'interpréter de maniere qu'il puisse avoir son effet
reuses.edition: Writings of Samuel Adams, ed. Cushing, II (1906)
reuses.note: The House turns Vattel's rules of interpretation against the Governor: after quoting "the celebrated author" that no contracting party may interpret at pleasure (apparently II.265), it quotes II.283 so that the charter's grant of legislative power must be read to take effect, not be nullified by Parliament's reserved power. The judge's page (421) is wrong: the passage is on p. 411; no source row covers this sentence, though the rule in the sentences before it has Wolff, Institutiones § 804 behind it.

The judge's date is wrong: this is the reply of 2 March 1773, on p. 452.

reuses.author: Daniel Leonard
reuses.label: verbatim
reuses.american:
The best writers upon the law of
nations tell us, that when a nation takes possession of a distant

reuses.vattel_1797: When a nation takes possession of a distant country, and settles a colony there, that country, though separated from the principal establishment, or mother-country, naturally becomes a part of the state, equally with its ancient possessions.
reuses.french: Lorsqu'une nation s'empare d'un pays éloigné , & y établit une colonie , ce pays , quoique séparé de l'établissement principal , fait naturellement partie de l'état ; tout comme ses anciennes possessions.

reuses.note: Leonard sets Vattel I.210, unnamed, as what 'the best writers upon the law of nations tell us', between 'The colonies are a part of the British empire' and the imperium in imperio argument, to conclude that the colonies are subject to Parliament. Author is Daniel Leonard; the judge's Jonathan Sewall follows the 1819 title page.
